issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent physical bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on anger, distrust, hypervigilance, and media avoidance after police violence but contains no corroborating threat or memory content about ongoing somatic injury, pain, disability, or bodily fragility. It stands out as a different trauma consequence than the remainder of the formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling used for excitement/distracting is weakly connected to the rest of the selected profile. The dominant formulation is Threat ↔ Negative Appraisals with trauma-memory-linked fear/anger and avoidance of feelings/media. Gambling for excitement does not clearly address the specific threat, memory, or appraisal pattern represented elsewhere, making it the least coherent maladaptive strategy in this set.

vignette: Samir Al-Fayed had been walking home from his evening run when two patrol vehicles mounted the curb and blocked his path. Officers shouted through open windows, misreading his raised hands as a challenge. When he tried to speak, a uniformed man lunged, pinning Samir to the wet asphalt. His cheek pressed against the grit, the thick rubber of a tactical glove pressed against his lips, and the copper taste of a bitten tongue filled his mouth. The encounter lasted less than four minutes, but Samir had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place where routines offered no protection. In the months that followed, the event did not fade. When the recollection returned, the taste of rubber and blood would flood his mouth before he could step back from the memory. He found himself pushing it away the moment it neared completion, letting the scene dissolve before he could piece together what happened next. Alongside this, a different response surfaced: when the memory finally broke through, he felt intense rage, a heat that tightened his throat and made his knuckles whiten. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, and that the uniform that day was simply one mask among many. He was certain that the world operated on hidden dangers, and that his own compliance during the arrest-standing still, swallowing his voice, following orders that felt degrading-had acted against who he was. These realities existed in him side by side, each occupying the same space without yielding to the other. He stopped allowing himself to feel. Strong negative feelings, whether fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, were treated as immediate intrusions. He avoided media that might spark them, turning off news apps, skipping television programs about policing, and closing any article that mentioned police encounters. He checked his surroundings constantly, eyes darting to doorways, windows, and street corners. He could not relax, even when he knew he was in a safe place, his muscles holding the posture of someone expecting a sudden charge. Before he felt comfortable anywhere, he always identified escape routes, counting exits, timing how long it would take to reach the sidewalk. His work as a social media manager required him to sit in glass-walled co-working spaces and client cafés, and these environments now demanded his full attention. He walked into meeting rooms and mapped his escape route before unloading his laptop. Clients noticed the distance in his posture, the way he flinched when a door slammed down the hall, the careful way he avoided his phone's notification sounds. Samir had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, and that his own compromised compliance during the arrest had violated his core values. He did not explain this to his wife, Leila. Instead, he built his days around emotional restraint and environmental control. Over the past ten months, the checking became automatic, the avoidance exhaustive. He missed team brainstorming sessions because he could not sit in rooms with limited exits. He stopped using public transit, switching to a car he drove alone to avoid unexpected stops. The strain accumulated in the silence between him and Leila, in the hollowed-out quality of his workdays. What finally brought Samir to seek help was a Tuesday afternoon when he found himself unable to type a single word of a client's campaign strategy. His hands had gone cold, his eyes darting to the café's front door as if waiting for boots to hit the pavement. He knew he could not keep building his life around fear. He was most afraid of losing his career entirely, but what he hoped for, however quietly, was to find a place where he could sit without counting the doors, where the past could stop tasting like copper in his mouth, and where he might finally remember who he was outside of survival.
